h2Outline: How cost of living is calculated

faq.question: How is cost of living calculated?
faq.answer: It is a price level, not a budget. The index used here comes from BEA Regional Price Parities, which measure the price of rent, goods and services in one metro against the national average of 100 — so a metro at 112 is 12% more expensive than the country as a whole.

faq.question: What is included in cost of living?
faq.answer: Rent, goods and services. Rent comes from HUD Fair Market Rent at county level, and it is the component that varies most between places. Income tax is not part of the price level and is handled separately, because two places at the same price level can leave you with very different amounts of money.

faq.question: Is cost of living the same as inflation?
faq.answer: No, and confusing the two is the most common error here. Inflation measures how prices change over time in one place; a cost-of-living index measures how prices differ between places at one point in time. CPI cannot tell you whether Austin is cheaper than San Francisco.

faq.question: What salary do I need in this city?
faq.answer: That is the reverse calculation, and it depends on household size as much as on the city. The living wage calculator solves for the gross salary a place requires rather than the cost a salary has to cover.

pages.title: Rent Affordability Calculator (2026)
pages.metaDescription: Find the highest rent your income can actually carry, then see how that figure lines up against real HUD market rents in your metro.

faq.question: How much rent can I afford on my salary?
faq.answer: The federal standard is 30% of gross income, which comes from the Brooke Amendment: 25% in 1969, raised to 30% in 1981. A household paying above 30% is officially cost burdened, and above 50% severely cost burdened.

faq.question: Is the 30% rule still realistic?
faq.answer: It is a policy threshold, not a market forecast. In the most expensive metros 30% of a median income does not reach the 40th-percentile rent, which is why this tool shows your ceiling next to the metro's actual rent rather than returning the percentage alone.

faq.question: What income do landlords require?
faq.answer: Most screening uses a gross multiple rather than a percentage: commonly three times the monthly rent in gross monthly income, which works out to a 33% ceiling. New York often uses 40x the monthly rent in annual income. What you can carry and what you will be approved for are different numbers.

faq.question: Does the 30% include utilities?
faq.answer: HUD publishes rent both with and without a utility allowance, and the gap runs from roughly $80 to over $250 a month depending on climate and unit type. A figure quoted without saying which one it is will be wrong by that much.

faq.question: How do I compare the cost of living between two cities?
faq.answer: Compare price levels, not budgets. Each metro carries a BEA Regional Price Parity against a national base of 100, so the ratio between two metros' figures is the real difference in what a month costs there.

faq.question: Does a higher salary in an expensive city leave me better off?
faq.answer: Not reliably. The price difference between two metros and the state income tax difference work in the same direction more often than people expect, so a raise that looks large in gross terms can be smaller than the cost gap it has to cover.

faq.question: Which costs differ most between cities?
faq.answer: Rent, by a wide margin. Goods and services vary far less because they move through national supply chains, which is why a comparison that averages everything together understates how much of the difference is housing.

faq.question: Is a cost of living comparison the same as a salary comparison?
faq.answer: No. A cost comparison tells you what a place charges; a salary comparison tells you what an income is worth there after tax. Both are needed, and the second is the one job offers usually omit.

faq.question: How do I compare job offers in two different cities?
faq.answer: Convert both to what they leave after tax, then measure each against what its city charges. An offer is better only if it wins on both, and a gross-to-gross comparison decides neither.

faq.question: How do I convert a salary to an hourly rate?
faq.answer: Divide the annual salary by the hours worked in a year. A standard full-time year is 2,080 hours — 40 hours over 52 weeks — so $95,000 becomes about $45.67 an hour before tax.

faq.question: Is 2,080 hours right for everyone?
faq.answer: It ignores paid leave. A salaried employee with three weeks off is still paid for 2,080 hours but works closer to 1,960, which raises the effective hourly rate by about 6%. A contractor paid only for hours worked has no such cushion.

faq.question: How do I convert hourly pay to a salary?
faq.answer: Multiply by the hours you actually work in a year rather than by 2,080. The distinction matters most for part-time and shift work, where the assumed number drives the whole answer.

faq.question: Should I compare offers by hourly rate or salary?
faq.answer: Neither on its own. An hourly rate ignores benefits and paid leave, and a salary ignores the hours behind it. Comparing what each leaves after tax in the place you would live is the only version that settles the question.

h2Outline: How a living wage is calculated

faq.question: What is a living wage?
faq.answer: The gross salary that covers a specific place's actual costs for a specific household. It is computed from local rent, goods, services and tax, unlike a minimum wage, which is a statutory floor set without reference to any of them.

faq.question: How is a living wage different from the minimum wage?
faq.answer: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 2009, which is $15,080 over a 2,080-hour year — below the poverty guideline for a household of two in every state. A living wage is an arithmetic result; a minimum wage is a legislated number.

faq.question: Does a living wage include savings?
faq.answer: No. It is a break-even figure covering costs without debt repayment, retirement saving beyond payroll deductions, or discretionary spending. Knowing how far an offer sits above the floor is a separate and more useful question.

faq.question: Why does household size change the answer so much?
faq.answer: Child care behaves like a second rent. For a household with two young children it exceeds housing costs in much of the country, which is why the gap between household types is usually larger than the gap between cities.

faq.question: How is income tax calculated?
faq.answer: Federal tax is bracketed: each slice of taxable income is taxed at its own rate, so the top rate applies only to the income above that threshold, never to the whole amount. State tax is then applied under that state's own rules.

faq.question: What is the difference between marginal and effective tax rate?
faq.answer: The marginal rate is what the next dollar is taxed at; the effective rate is total tax divided by total income. The effective rate is always lower, and mistaking one for the other is why people overestimate what a raise costs them.

faq.question: Do all states tax income?
faq.answer: No. Nine levy no income tax on wages. Of the rest, some apply a single flat rate and others a progressive schedule with a top rate above 10%.

faq.question: Is income tax the same as what comes out of my paycheck?
faq.answer: No. What is withheld comes from the W-4 on file and is an estimate; the liability calculated here is the actual amount owed for the year. The refund or bill in April is the difference between the two.

pages.title: Take Home Pay Calculator (2026)
pages.metaDescription: See what is left of a gross salary after federal, state, Social Security and Medicare — yearly and monthly. Free, no sign-up.

faq.question: How do I calculate take-home pay?
faq.answer: Subtract federal income tax, state income tax, Social Security at 6.2% and Medicare at 1.45% from gross pay. Social Security and Medicare together are FICA, 7.65% for an employee.

faq.question: Why is my take-home pay so much lower than my salary?
faq.answer: On a $95,000 salary the deductions run to roughly a quarter of the figure, and the exact amount depends on the state by as much as $7,167 a year. Pre-tax deductions like a 401(k) and health premiums change it further.

faq.question: What is the difference between biweekly and semi-monthly pay?
faq.answer: Biweekly is every two weeks: 26 checks a year, with two months containing three of them. Semi-monthly is twice a month: 24 checks of identical size. At the same salary the biweekly check is smaller, and the two extra checks close the gap.

faq.question: Do self-employed people pay more?
faq.answer: Yes. An employer pays a matching 7.65% FICA that never appears on a payslip. A self-employed person pays both halves — 15.3% — which is the largest single difference between an employee and a contractor at the same gross figure.

faq.question: How do I calculate sales tax?
faq.answer: Multiply the pre-tax price by the combined rate, which is the state rate plus any county, city and special district rates. The combined rate is what you pay, and it is often well above the state rate alone.

faq.question: Which states have no sales tax?
faq.answer: Five: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon. Alaska is the exception that matters — it has no state sales tax but permits local ones, so parts of the state do charge it.

faq.question: Why does the rate change within one state?
faq.answer: Because local jurisdictions stack their own rates on top of the state rate. Two addresses a few miles apart can face different combined rates, which is why a state-level figure is not enough to price a purchase.

faq.question: Does sales tax affect the cost of living?
faq.answer: Yes, and it is the part most cost-of-living comparisons leave out. A state with no income tax that charges a high combined sales tax recovers much of the difference on everything you buy.

faq.answer: Assessed value multiplied by the local rate, often expressed in mills. Assessed value is set by the county and is frequently lower than market value, so applying a rate to a sale price overstates the bill.

faq.question: What is included in a monthly house payment?
faq.answer: Principal, interest, property tax, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance where the down payment is under 20% — together known as PITI. A figure covering only principal and interest understates the real payment substantially.

faq.question: What is PMI and when does it stop?
faq.answer: Private mortgage insurance is charged when the down payment falls below 20% of the price. On a conventional loan it can be cancelled once equity reaches 20%, and lenders must remove it automatically at 22%.

faq.question: How much does the interest rate change the payment?

faq.answer: No. Maintenance, conventionally budgeted at 1% of value a year, and HOA dues where they apply sit outside the payment entirely and outside every lender calculation.

faq.question: How much house can I afford?
faq.answer: Conventional underwriting applies two ratios to gross monthly income: 28% for housing alone and 36% for housing plus all other debt. The second is the binding one for most buyers.

faq.question: What is the 28/36 rule?
faq.answer: A guideline, not a law. The Qualified Mortgage standard allows debt-to-income up to 43%, FHA lending routinely approves above that, and automated underwriting has pushed some approvals near 50%. The conservative answer and the maximum answer are far apart.

faq.question: How do car and student loans affect it?
faq.answer: They count fully against the back-end ratio while contributing nothing toward the house. Two households with identical incomes and a $600 monthly difference in car payments qualify for roughly $100,000 of price difference.

faq.question: Is the price I qualify for the price I should pay?
faq.answer: No. Closing costs run 2% to 5% of the purchase price and are paid at the table, and maintenance is conventionally budgeted at 1% of home value a year. Neither reduces what you qualify for; both reduce what you should want.
